guide.title: Routing and failover
guide.subtitle: What happens when the primary provider has a bad hour
guide.excerpt: Routes are ordered by priority and weighted within a connection. The point of the arrangement is that a provider rejecting sends degrades into slower sending, not into silence.

p: Connections on a route carry a priority. The highest-priority connection that is healthy and still inside its pacing budget takes the message. Only when it cannot do so does the next one in line get it.
This is the arrangement that makes a second provider worth configuring. A single connection with no fallback has exactly one failure mode, and it is total.

sections.h: Weight spreads load within a connection
p: Several sender numbers can be bound to one connection, each with a weight. Messages are distributed across them by that weight, so a number carrying a heavier share takes proportionally more traffic.
Because provider limits are typically per number, spreading across numbers within a connection is often the simplest way to raise real throughput without changing providers.

A connection that keeps rejecting sends is taken out of rotation rather than being retried indefinitely. Without that, one misconfigured connection at the top of a route becomes a single point of failure for every message behind it — the position where a mistake costs the most.

list: It does not guarantee delivery. It changes which provider carries a message, not whether the destination carrier accepts it.
It does not repair a bad route. If every connection on the route has the same misconfiguration, failover has nowhere to go.
It does not cover email or WhatsApp. Automatic failover is implemented for the SMS channel.
